# A Short Note on the Existence of a Fixed Point

## Abstract

We prove the existence of a unique fixed point for a contraction mapping on a
complete metric space, and discuss a simple application to the solution of a
nonlinear equation.

## 1 Introduction

Let $(X, d)$ be a complete metric space. A map $f: X \to X$ is called a
contraction if there exists a constant $k \in [0, 1)$ such that

$$ d(f(x), f(y)) \le k \, d(x, y) \quad \text{for all } x, y \in X. $$

Banach's contraction principle states that every contraction on a complete
metric space admits exactly one fixed point.

## 2 Main Result

**Theorem 2.1.** Every contraction $f$ on a complete metric space $X$ has a
unique fixed point $x^*$, and the sequence defined by

$$ x_{n+1} = f(x_n) $$

converges to $x^*$ for any starting point $x_0 \in X$.

## 3 Application

Consider the integral equation

$$ u(x) = g(x) + \lambda \int_a^b K(x, t) \, u(t) \, dt, \qquad 0 < |\lambda| < 1, $$

where $K$ is continuous on $[a, b] \times [a, b]$. Under a Lipschitz
condition on the kernel, the right-hand side defines a contraction, and hence
a unique solution $u$ exists by the theorem above. The error after $n$
iterations is bounded by

$$ \| u_n - u \| \le \frac{k^n}{1 - k} \, \| u_1 - u_0 \|. $$

This completes the proof.
